worked_solution:
A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

Now, let's consider each equation:

- The first equation is

$$
(2xy+5)\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+7)\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

 
Therefore, the functions $P$ and $Q$ are

$$
P(x,y)=2xy+5,\,Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+7.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+5) \\  & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+7) \\  & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,✓
$$

 
Thus, equation I is exact.

- The second equation is

$$
({y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x+(xy+1)\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

Therefore, the functions $P$ and $Q$ are

$$
P(x,y)={y}^{2}+x,\,Q(x,y)=xy+1.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+x) \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+1) \\  & =y\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,\times 
$$

Thus, equation II is not exact.

- The third equation is

$$
(5y-3x)\,\text{d}y-(y-2x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Therefore, the functions $P$ and $Q$ are

$$
P(x,y)=-(y-2x)=2x-y,\,Q(x,y)=5y-3x.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-y) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y-3x) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

 
So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,\times 
$$

Thus, equation III is not exact.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".
